newsitem.title: GERMANY: US economist says Buba rate cut could help dollar.
newsitem.headline: US economist says Buba rate cut could help dollar.

text.p: A top U.S. economist on Thursday criticised the Bundesbank for keeping interest rates at unsuitably high levels and said another significant cut could help the dollar appreciate significantly.
In an interview with German weekly news magazine Wirtschafts Woche, independent economist Ruediger Dornbusch said German interest rates were still too high in light of sluggish economic growth.
Saying that Germany's problems can, in part, be blamed on the Bundesbank, Dornbusch added:

"The big problem is the completely incomprehensible insistence by the Bundesbank which is again looking at money supply instead of looking at the economy, which wants to grow by four percent. For a quasi dead economy without inflation, interest rates are still too high."

Dornbusch, an economics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said that if the Bundesbank would cut its key discount rate by another 50 basis points to two percent, "this could boost the dollar by another 10 percent."

"In the U.S. no one would be against another dollar appreciation if there would be another interest rate cut and strong European growth. To only talk the dollar higher is not the right way," he added.

The Bundesbank is holding its final policy-setting meeting of the year today, but the majority view is for the central bank to keep all key interest rates, including the 2.50 percent discount, the 4.50 percent Lombard and the three percent main money market rate, the repo, steady.
The Bundesbank never tires of stressing that its primary mandate is to keep inflation in check, not to prop up a sluggish economy by announcing politically motivated interest rate adjustments.
But recently a number of Bundesbank council members have also stressed that the German economy, largely driven by exports, would benefit from a slightly stronger dollar.
This talk has often helped hoist the dollar back above the critical 1.50 mark level. On Thursday the dollar was trading at 1.5566 marks.

On the other hand Dornbusch is confident that the U.S. central bank, the Fed, will not take preventative action but will only nudge interest rates slightly higher when real signs of inflationary dangers appear on the horizon.
"But this will be at least six months off," he added.
